Lane 301, Sancheng Fang, Tongfu Li: on the wall of the archway house at the lane mouth, the side facing the street, a signboard was nailed to the corner, and across it in large characters ran the words “Western-Medicine Clinic — Qin Chuan'an.” Below, unlike some of the private clinics in the Settlement, it did not list pediatrics, gynecology, internal and surgical medicine and all the rest, the sort of thing that leaves one feeling the doctor takes on anything and is not quite to be trusted. The small print beneath the sign was simple enough: it gave only the consulting hours, one o'clock to seven in the afternoon, and house calls by appointment.

Up in the archway house, Qin Chuan'an was worrying. These last two days he had begun to suspect the clinic was being watched. Across the street, at the mouth of the lane, a cigarette seller had suddenly appeared, one he had never seen before; and out on his house calls he always felt someone tailing him behind. He was not so certain whether that unfamiliar face was one he had glimpsed several times about the neighborhood.

Was it merely because he had come forward to put up the surety bond? That, at least, had been thought out in advance, with a passable pretext concocted for it. A surety bond was a formality in any case, a favor done between relatives, between friends. Standing surety for Liang Shichao was more legitimate still, for the man already helped out at the clinic.

Old Fang had never imagined the rescue would go so smoothly; within a few days there had been word. A few days earlier he had telephoned the clinic to tell Qin Chuan'an that his own situation was very dangerous, that the enemy was hunting him everywhere, and then he had fallen wholly silent.

That was proof enough that the enemy knew a great deal. Qin Chuan'an had no idea how the rescue work would proceed, and could only wait. Yet, against all expectation, the people really were let out. The clinic received the notices of release, and still he could not find Old Fang.

Qin Chuan'an was a surgeon. For several years before this he had been a resident physician at the nearby German Hospital, and had then come out on his own to open the clinic; the public reason was that the German Hospital required its resident physicians to be single, though of course there was another reason as well. The original arrangement with Old Fang had been that he would come forward to stand surety for Liang Shichao only, and that the others would be provided for separately, but then Old Fang himself had run into trouble.

What was astonishing was that the Judge Advocate's office of the Garrison Command actually approached him: since the others in the same case had been slow to submit their surety documents, would Dr. Qin be willing to stand surety for all the co-defendants? With the New Year almost upon them, the lockup wished to let these people go home a little sooner. It was a very strange thing indeed. Since when had the Kuomintang's Longhua lockup grown so tender-hearted? Standing surety for Liang Shichao was legitimate; standing surety for the other comrades was as good as telling the enemy outright that these people were all of one band. But he was anxious to save them, and so he made a show of reluctance, and when the other side tried once more to persuade him, he agreed and signed the surety papers.

He had not expected things to go so smoothly, and on the day of the release Qin Chuan'an had even been especially glad. Cui Wentai drove, and together they brought Liang Shichao and the wounded Lin Shi back to the clinic, and the other comrades all came out of prison without a hitch. But the moment he was back at the clinic, his gladness left him. Liang Shichao told him quietly that there was a mole. So secret a meeting — how had the agents learned of it? And in such detail, too; that fellow surnamed You had even produced a pair of dice.
“If the enemy knew so much, why would they release these comrades?”

No sooner had Qin Chuan'an asked the question than the thought struck him: if the organization had been penetrated from within, if there was a mole, then the release might mean some larger plot. But he did not know what to do; Old Fang had vanished, and the link to the higher-ups was cut.
And it was not only the unfamiliar faces that had turned up outside the clinic that worried him.

That morning, when he came to the ward, Lin Shi said he wanted to make a telephone call to the bank. Lin Shi's public identity was that of a clerk at the Rentai Bank Company, and after so many days from arrest to release he ought to get in touch with the bank where he worked. Qin Chuan'an thought nothing of it, and was about to call Liang Shichao to help Lin Shi to the consulting room, but Lin Shi said he could manage on his own.

The clinic was very quiet these days. The New Year was coming; apart from Lin Shi there were no inpatients, and since it was outside consulting hours not even the nurses had come on duty. Qin Chuan'an took the chance to talk a while with Liang Shichao.
When Liang Shichao heard that Lin Shi had gone off to make the call by himself, he said only, coldly: “So now he can walk.”

The call went on a long time. Back in the ward, Lin Shi handed Qin Chuan'an a letter and asked him to help post it. The addressee was Assistant Manager Wu of the Zhonghui Trust Bank. After all this to-ing and fro-ing, Lin Shi's fever rose again, and once he lay down he was soon asleep.

Qin Chuan'an carried the letter to the consulting room. The consulting room was up in the archway house, with windows open on both sides, toward the street and into the lane, so that it was very bright. He stood at the window facing the street and looked out. The cigarette seller had come on duty; the cigarette case slung about him, he did not hawk his wares but leaned against a telephone pole across the way, smoking one himself.
He was still considering how to slip the letter into the pillar-box across the street without drawing attention when Liang Shichao came in.
“Dr. Qin, don't be in a hurry to send that letter off. You'd best open it and take a look.”
“Why?”
“Why—” Liang Shichao hesitated a moment. “Do you remember I told you that day I suspected there was a spy inside the organization?”

“You suspect Comrade Lin Shi?” Qin Chuan'an was a little troubled; the street outside the clinic might already be under the enemy's watch, and if there was an agent within the clinic too, then the place would be no different from the lockup.

“I've suspected him all along. He's shamming illness. In the jail I saw his wound; it wasn't so serious. Why lie there in a stupor all day, moaning in his sleep, without a shred of revolutionary will? The instant he was in the clinic he perked up, telephoning and writing letters.”
Qin Chuan'an was a doctor, and he did not credit such a suspicion: “With a gunshot wound, every body reacts differently.”

“The agents were very solicitous of him, too — they went to the trouble of fetching a military surgeon from the Garrison Command to look at his wound and change the dressing; at his interrogations they used no torture, and though they questioned him several times, each time was brief. Even the warder who took him out was polite to him.”
“Is that all?”
“Isn't that enough? The struggle is so tangled just now that we must be on guard against any sign at all.”

But Qin Chuan'an would not agree to open the envelope; he felt he had no right to suspect a comrade so. Liang Shichao had always trusted Qin Chuan'an, but the doctor did not know what had happened after the arrests, and turn it over as he might, Liang Shichao could not dispel the doubt in his heart; and so he demanded that a provisional Party branch meeting be called.

This provisional Party branch, besides the comrades who had been arrested, included Qin Chuan'an, Cui Wentai, and Tian Fei. The latter two had not originally worked on the same line as Qin Chuan'an, and were strangers to one another; but on the day he and Tian Fei fled the market together, they had happened to see Cui Wentai getting into his own car. All three were somewhat dazed, not knowing what on earth had happened; they needed first to find a place to collect themselves and think what to do next, and Qin Chuan'an had Cui Wentai drive to the clinic, which he judged should be safer, since the agents might not think at once to connect a surgeon with the Communists.

After Old Fang disappeared, the three of them kept in touch. On the night before the comrades in prison were to be released, Cui Wentai had volunteered to drive out and bring them back. In these days they were like kites with cut strings, and could only make the clinic their meeting point, gathering to hearten one another. Tian Fei proposed forming a provisional Party branch: only in unity was there fighting strength. This everyone agreed to; if they lost contact with the organization, then by organizing themselves they could still carry on the work.
But now, at this moment, Qin Chuan'an would not agree to hold the branch meeting. He felt there were too many strange signs in the streets around the clinic; it was not normal.

Liang Shichao was somewhat angry. With anyone else he would long since have flared up, but he could not do so with Dr. Qin, who was a meticulous man and had, moreover, saved his life. He mastered his feelings, turned, and went out.

An hour later he was back, and not alone: Cui Wentai and Tian Fei came behind him. The three entered the consulting room, and it was Tian Fei who spoke first, saying gravely to Qin Chuan'an: “You must hand over the letter. The provisional Party branch has decided to open it.”

Qin Chuan'an looked out of the window. It was near noon, and the sun fell on the houses along the street opposite, under whose windows hung a good many salted fish, cured pork, and wind-dried chickens. Tomorrow was New Year's Eve, and every household was busy with its preparations. People came and went in the street, carrying strings of New Year goods in their hands.

Since it was the will of all of them, he decided to comply. He took the letter from the drawer, and Tian Fei snatched it up and made to tear it open, but Cui Wentai stopped him. On the stove in the consulting room a kettle of water was heating, and when it boiled the steam came billowing from the spout. Liang Shichao held the sealed flap of the letter to the spout, and in a little while the glue on the flap melted. He lifted the flap, drew out the sheet, and handed the letter to Qin Chuan'an.
Assistant Manager Wu Zuomin, for your esteemed perusal:

We had arranged to meet with you on the tenth of this month, but a matter prevented my coming. I further learned by telephone that the renewal of the safe-deposit box was to be conveyed by letter. As follows:

I beg to state: safe-deposit box No. 279 is hereby to be kept in use until March 11, all the several charges pertaining thereto to be settled together before the term expires. I trust you will at once receive and approve this. With respect, I remain.
Qin Chuan'an read the letter and said nothing. Tian Fei took it, finished reading, and at once let out a soft cry: “Just as I thought.”
“Just as you thought?” Liang Shichao asked quickly.
“The tenth of this month — isn't that the very day of the meeting at the market, the day the enemy arrested us?”
“And what does that show?” Liang Shichao asked again.

“A secret meeting, the higher-ups setting an urgent assignment, so important a matter — and he still had the leisure to arrange a rendezvous with someone. There's certainly something wrong with him.” Since the enemy had charged into the library to make the arrests, Tian Fei, though he had gotten clear, grew more and more agitated at every turn.
“That shows nothing at all.” Qin Chuan'an signaled to them not to be hasty. “Comrade Lin Shi's public identity is that of a bank clerk to begin with; that is his everyday work.”
He used the word “Comrade” deliberately, meaning to put them on their guard.

“He's only just been released, wounded and in hospital — does the everyday work of a bank call for telephoning and letter-writing so urgently? And look, even after his arrest he could still be carrying his seal on him.” Tian Fei thought himself very sharp, and pointed to the personal seal stamped at the foot of the letter.
“Then what do we do now?” put in Cui Wentai.
At this the several of them were at a loss. An internal investigation must have the organization's approval; that was discipline.
“We can't reach the higher-ups, so we'll get to the bottom of it ourselves.” Tian Fei was growing worked up.
“Get to the bottom of it how?” Liang Shichao glanced at Qin Chuan'an.
“We should take control of him first; we can't leave him alone in the ward.” Tian Fei had not finished speaking before he was leading the way to the ward.
The three entered the ward. Cui Wentai shut the door, Liang Shichao took up a place by the window, and Tian Fei bent over Lin Shi and asked: “What's in the safe-deposit box?”
Lin Shi blinked, as if not yet fully awake, somewhat dazed.
“Who is this Assistant Manager Wu?” Tian Fei lowered his voice.
Lin Shi thought a moment: “Assistant Manager Wu of the Zhonghui Trust Bank?”

“You were to meet on the tenth of this month — did you mean to go and see him after the meeting broke up?” Tian Fei fired off his questions like a string of firecrackers, though there was no logic linking them.
Liang Shichao cut in: “Why do you think the enemy discovered our secret meeting?”
“Why do you think they discovered it?” Lin Shi countered with a smile.
“This is a formal questioning of you by the provisional Party branch. Kindly be serious—” Cui Wentai remarked from across the room, propped against the door.

The remark was not the least bit serious, Liang Shichao thought, and he waved a hand at Cui Wentai. “We discussed this very question back in the enemy's lockup, and the conclusion was that there is very likely a spy of the enemy's within the organization.”

“It can't yet be called a conclusion.” Lin Shi's tone was calm. “A lapse in the work, or a leak through some other channel — these possibilities all exist. It calls for a strict investigation through the organization, under the leadership of the higher-ups.”
“The higher-ups can't be reached; and even if they could be reached now, we can't rush into contact — we must first root out the mole.”
“These two comrades,” Lin Shi pointed at Tian Fei and Cui Wentai, “ought not to be here. Comrades who weren't arrested coming to see us like this now — it isn't quite proper.”
Tian Fei bridled, stepped forward and flung the quilt off Lin Shi: “Sit up and answer the questions properly.”
“The owner of the safe-deposit box is a customer of the bank,” Lin Shi said, sitting up and leaning against the head of the bed. “I work at a bank.”

“Don't lie to us. You work at the Rentai Bank Company, and the safe-deposit box is at the Zhonghui Trust Bank. It's no bank customer — the box is one you rented yourself.” Cui Wentai, at a distance, smiled with a touch of triumph.
“The way I see it, until we open that box and see what's really inside, you won't tell the truth.” Tian Fei's voice rose the more he spoke.
Cui Wentai gave the other two a look. The three left the room, and Tian Fei turned back to Lin Shi: “Don't you move.”
Back in the consulting room, Tian Fei asked: “What do we do?”
They were all at a loss. Qin Chuan'an had just started to speak when Liang Shichao cut him off: “We've come this far — then let's see it through to the end.”
“We can't lay hands on him, surely?” Tian Fei was a little hesitant.
“Absolutely not.” Qin Chuan'an was firm.
Seeing them all stand there stupefied for the moment, Cui Wentai said: “Let's tie him up first; if he really is an agent, he might just make a run for it.”
Liang Shichao thought it over: “Tying him up is no bad thing — let's see whether he takes fright.”
The three rushed back to the ward once more.

Qin Chuan'an listened a while in the corridor; there was no sound of struggle. Lin Shi had not resisted, he thought. He went back to the consulting room, found a record of Schubert's, and meant to listen to some music, but no sooner had he opened the gramophone than he closed it again. He looked out of the window, his heart growing more and more uneasy.

All at once he caught sight of a woman getting down from a rickshaw across the street — a lined gown of brocade satin, a purple woolen overcoat, a box of Guanshengyuan pastries in her hand, done up like a wealthy wife off to visit relatives for the New Year. She stood on the curb, turned her head to look both ways, and just as she was about to cross, glanced up once more toward the clinic; only then did Qin Chuan'an recognize Ling Wen. Had Liang Shichao told her, too? He wondered at it. This was chaos indeed: unable to reach the higher-ups, the comrades went their own way and made his place a liaison station. The trouble was that just now the clinic was very likely under the agents' watch.
The nurses had not yet come on duty, and he went down himself to open the door.
“Dr. Qin,” Ling Wen said, standing at the door with a smile, “I've come to see Mr. Lin—”
“There are no outsiders here,” Qin Chuan'an told her once she was inside. “It's not consulting hours yet; the nurses haven't come on duty.”
As they went up the stairs, Ling Wen told Qin Chuan'an that Old Yi had sent her to inform them all: he had made contact with the higher-ups.
“That's a relief,” said Qin Chuan'an with heartfelt gladness. “I was just at my wits' end.”
“What's the matter?”
Once they were in the consulting room, Qin Chuan'an told Ling Wen what had just happened.
“This won't do at all,” Ling Wen said at once. “Let me go and see first.”
The moment she entered the ward, she saw the three men gathered around a chair in the middle of the room; in the chair sat Lin Shi, his arms bound to the chair-back.
Ling Wen led off at once: “Untie him.”
“We can't; he's a mole.” Of these men, only Liang Shichao knew her, and he added, “—very likely.”
“An internal investigation must follow the higher-ups' instructions.”
“The higher-ups can't be reached.”
“They've been reached.”
At these words everyone in the room looked at her, and Tian Fei's grip on Lin Shi's hand loosened too.
“The higher-ups sent someone to make contact with Old Yi,” Ling Wen told them, a little excited. “The meeting went off smoothly.”
“Did the higher-ups say we could resume work?” Tian Fei asked eagerly.

“Undisciplined and disorganized, the lot of you — gathering as you please, investigating comrades as you please, running wild. Comrade Tian Fei, the meeting place upstairs at the market was one the organization had you arrange; are we all to suspect you on that account?” Ling Wen glared at him.
Tian Fei could not help feeling a little wronged, thinking that he had, after all, arranged the meeting place on Old Fang's instructions.
Lin Shi looked mildly at Tian Fei, then turned to Ling Wen and asked: “What does Old Yi say?”

“Old Yi thinks we should meet and confer as soon as possible. Before the organization begins its internal investigation, each of us must prepare, recalling clearly all the circumstances before and after the arrests, so as to report them truthfully to the higher-ups when the time comes.”
“Ask Old Yi to tell the higher-ups that I want to go back to work in the Soviet area,” Liang Shichao said in earnest.
“He was a Red Army commander to begin with, and came to Shanghai for treatment; he can't get back for the time being,” Qin Chuan'an explained to Ling Wen.

“Old Fang said he had reported my situation to the organization, and then all at once called me to the meeting at the market for a temporary assignment. And now, after all this, I can't get back again.”

“The higher-ups arranged for you to take part in this assignment; there must be a purpose in it.” Qin Chuan'an turned again to them all: “Everyone, think carefully about your own identity. The organization chose us for a reason. If this goes on, even the clinic's nurses will grow suspicious.”
Liang Shichao said nothing. He had left half his life in Shanghai, and it was Dr. Qin who had saved him.
“By the way, you should rest and recover in peace — you can stay here a few days,” Lin Shi said, looking at Liang Shichao with a smile.

Liang Shichao had never been able to abide the sight of Lin Shi, who had lain about all day in the lockup, plainly a little afraid of the enemy. Even with the investigation of Lin Shi suspended for now, Liang Shichao still had his misgivings: “I've rested and recovered too long already. In a situation like this, how can I rest easy?”
